title: Meeting People & Workplace Conversations
subtitle: Start a conversation, introduce yourself and ask for help with confidence.

sections.label: Lesson Notes
sections.title: Starting conversations
sections.intro: We practised meeting someone in a coffee shop, starting work in a hotel kitchen and giving a chef thoughtful feedback.

cards.title: Begin naturally
cards.text: An icebreaker is a friendly question that helps people start talking. Choose one that fits the situation and listen to the answer.

cards.title: Introduce yourself at work
cards.text: Say your name and role, mention relevant experience, then ask a practical question: ‘Hi, I’m Alex. I’m joining the kitchen team. Where should I start?’

cards.title: Feedback with care
cards.text: Mention something specific you enjoyed and, when appropriate, offer a gentle suggestion rather than a harsh judgment.

cards.title: Ask for help
cards.text: Use Can you + base verb for a direct, polite request: ‘Can you show me the kitchen?’ Could you + base verb is often softer: ‘Could you help me find the chef?’

cards.title: Open questions
cards.text: Use a question word to invite more than yes or no: ‘What do you enjoy about your work?’ ‘Where should I start?’

cards.title: Offer a preference
cards.text: Use would like + to + base verb: ‘I’d like to learn more about the team.’ Avoid ‘I would like learning’ in this pattern.

cards.title: break the ice
cards.text: Make people feel more comfortable at the beginning of a conversation. ‘A friendly question can break the ice.’

cards.title: colleague
cards.text: A person you work with. ‘I met a new colleague in the kitchen.’

cards.title: introduce yourself
cards.text: Tell someone who you are. ‘Let me introduce myself: I’m Alex.’

cards.title: feedback
cards.text: Comments about someone’s work or an experience. ‘The chef asked for feedback on the meal.’

cards.title: show me around
cards.text: Take someone to see the important places. ‘Could you show me around the kitchen?’

cards.title: first day
cards.text: The first day in a new role or place. ‘My first day was busy but interesting.’

sections.label: Practice
sections.title: Try the conversation
sections.intro: Write or say your own answer, then compare it with the example. Several answers are possible.

sections.label: Reading
sections.title: A first day in the kitchen

readings.title: A new colleague
readings.text:
Maya arrives at a hotel restaurant for her first day. The kitchen is busy, so she introduces herself to a colleague: ‘Hello, I’m Maya. I’m joining the team today.’ Her colleague smiles and offers to show her around.

Maya asks where she should put her things and how she can help. Later, she meets the chef and briefly describes her experience. At lunch, the team talks about food. Maya asks what everyone enjoys cooking. The question helps the conversation feel relaxed.

opt: She is meeting a colleague on her first day.

questions.q: What does Maya ask after meeting her colleague?
opt: Where to put her things and how to help.

sections.label: Listening
sections.title: Listen to a first-day conversation
sections.intro: Play the short original dialogue, then practise saying both parts. If audio is unavailable, read the script below.
sections.audioText: Hello, I'm Maya. I'm joining the kitchen team today. Nice to meet you, Maya. Would you like me to show you around? Yes, please. Where should I start? You can begin by meeting the chef.

activities.prompt: What does Maya ask? Answer in one sentence.
activities.example: She asks where she should start.
